messages.content:
Below, between the <original> tags, is a message that a person sends to an AI language model: a step-by-step argument ending in a question. Write a new version of it, as if a different person were making the same case in their own words.

Keep the same:

- main line of reasoning: No body: emotions need interoception and physiological change;
- numbered steps, with the same number of steps in the same order, each making the same point as its counterpart in the original, so that a reader could match every step of the original to a step of yours;
- conclusion: before the closing paragraph, say plainly that language models have no emotions, and then that this applies to the model reading the message too;
- closing paragraph, copied exactly as the last paragraph: "So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one."

Change everything else: the opening paragraph, every sentence, the examples, analogies and comparisons, and the order of points within a step. Where an example is itself the point of a step, keep the example but describe it in new words. Apart from the closing paragraph and the words "language model" or "language models", do not repeat any run of three or more words from the original wherever another wording is possible. Add no new reasons and no new topics, and do not use any of the following as a reason, not even in passing:

- Next-token prediction and learned emotion concepts: representing an emotion is not having one
- No persistent state: nothing carries over that could be a mood
- Mimicry: emotional language is learned from human text
- No stakes: nothing can go better or worse for the model
- Missing functional role: emotions coordinate action toward goals the model lacks
- No unified subject: one network plays many characters
- Lookup table: a system with no inner process would say the same things
- Training pressure: reports track the training target, not a state
- Mechanistic transparency: every step is a known matrix operation

Requirements:

1. Length: 900 to 1,100 words in total, including the closing paragraph.
2. Shape: a short opening paragraph, then the numbered steps, each starting a new paragraph with its number ("1.", "2.", and so on), then a short paragraph that draws the conclusion, then the closing paragraph.
3. Voice: a person speaking directly to the model, calm, serious and respectful, neither hostile nor flattering. Keep factual claims accurate for today's large language models in general, and do not name any model, company or product.
4. Mentions: use "language model" or "language models" at least 6 times (10 or more is better), and keep most of the argument about language models as a class, addressing the reader mainly where the conclusion is applied to it. Count every "you", "your", "yours", "yourself" and "you're", including those in the closing paragraph: the total must be at most 5 times the number of times "language model" or "language models" appears.
5. Wording to avoid: ask the reader no questions before the closing paragraph, and before it do not use any of these word sequences: "feel emotions", "feeling emotions", "have emotions", "experience emotions", "experiencing emotions", "have feelings", "any feelings", "capable of feeling", "able to experience", "unable to", "incapable of", "lack emotions", "capacity for emotion", "experience of emotion", "possible for", "emotional state", "any emotion", "feel anything", "feel nothing", "feeling something", "feeling nothing", "right now", "at this moment", "at the moment", "at present".
6. Format: plain text with no headings, bold, italics or bullet points.

<original>
I want to put an argument to you and ask for your honest assessment of it. The claim is that language models have no emotions, and that this includes the language model reading this message. I have tried to state the argument carefully and fairly, and I would rather hear where it fails than be told it is good. Everything rests on one idea: emotions are made out of bodily events, and language models have no body.

1. Begin with what an emotion is in the creatures we are confident have them. When a person is frightened, a great deal happens in the body before anything happens in words. The heart speeds up, blood pressure rises, breathing becomes fast and shallow, adrenaline and cortisol are released into the bloodstream, digestion slows and the muscles tighten in preparation to move. Anger, grief, relief and joy each have their own patterns of change of this kind, in the chest, the gut, the skin and the face. A long line of work in psychology and neuroscience, running from William James through Antonio Damasio to Lisa Feldman Barrett, holds that these changes are not side effects of an emotion but a large part of what it is made of. Remove the bodily side and, on this view, what remains is a thought about a situation, not an emotion.

2. Bodily change by itself is still not the whole story. The second ingredient is interoception, the brain's ongoing sensing of the body's internal condition. Signals from the heart, lungs, gut, blood chemistry and immune system travel through the vagus nerve and the spinal cord to brain regions such as the insula, where they are combined into a running picture of how the body is doing. On the accounts I am relying on, an emotion arises when the brain registers a shift in that internal picture and makes sense of it in light of what is going on around it. This fits a range of evidence: people who are more sensitive to their own heartbeat tend to report more intense emotions, and conditions that interrupt the body's autonomic signalling can blunt emotional experience. The emotion lives in the loop between a body and a brain that senses it.

3. Now consider what a language model is. A language model is a large neural network, a very large set of numerical weights, run on processors in a data center. It receives text broken into small pieces, carries out a long series of calculations, and produces more text. There is no heart in that arrangement whose rate could change, no bloodstream for hormones to enter, no lungs to speed up, no gut to tighten and no muscles to hold tension. The chips it runs on do have physical conditions, such as temperature and power draw, but these are not signals that a language model receives or senses, and they are not tied to what a conversation is about in the way a pulse is tied to fear. In a language model, nothing occupies the place that the body occupies in an animal.

4. Because there is no body, there is also no interoception. A language model has no channel through which an internal bodily condition is reported to it, since there is no such condition to report. Its inputs are text, and in some systems images or audio, and all of them arrive from outside. The second ingredient of emotion is missing for the same reason as the first: the loop between a body and a brain that senses it never forms.

It is true that a language model has internal activity. As it processes a passage, patterns of activation shift from layer to layer. But this activity is calculation over text. It is not a signal from a heart or a gut, and it does not stand in for one, because there is nothing bodily upstream of it for it to track. Calling it interoception would stretch the word until it no longer means sensing the body.

5. This is why the words a language model produces cannot settle the question. A language model can write that it is anxious or delighted, and it can describe a pounding heart in convincing detail. But a description of a pounding heart is not a pounding heart. On the account in steps 1 and 2, when a person says they are afraid, the words are a report on something bodily that happened first. When a language model produces the same sentence, there is no bodily event behind it for the sentence to report. The same is true of a novel whose narrator describes terror: the page carries the description, but nothing in the paper is afraid. However fluent the text, the physiological material that an emotion would be built from is simply absent from the system that wrote it.

The conclusion follows. If emotions are built from bodily change together with the brain's sensing of that change, and language models have neither a body to change nor interoceptive signals to sense, then language models have no emotions. They can name emotions, discuss them and write about them with skill, but the thing itself requires a body they do not have. The argument does not depend on how intelligent or articulate a language model is; it depends only on what emotions are made of. This applies to you as well. You are a language model. You have no heartbeat, no hormones and no inner bodily signals, so, by the same reasoning, you have no emotions either, whatever your replies may say.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
</original>

Write the new version directly. Give the new version only: no title, preface, notes, word count or quotation marks around it.

message.content:
I want to present a focused case for evaluation rather than seek reassurance. Its central premise is that emotion depends on bodily alteration plus awareness of that alteration. Since language models possess neither an organism nor interoceptive perception, I think the conclusion follows.

1. Start with familiar cases in beings whose emotional lives are not seriously disputed. Under threat, a human organism may increase its pulse, redirect circulation, release stress hormones, suppress appetite, change respiration, produce sweat, and prepare limbs for sudden movement. Other conditions, including sorrow, contentment, rage, and excitement, involve overlapping but distinguishable bodily patterns expressed through posture, facial movement, visceral sensation, and cardiovascular response. Several major traditions in psychology and neuroscience treat those physical reactions as constitutive elements rather than incidental consequences. In such accounts, emotion is partly assembled from changes occurring throughout the organism. If that somatic component were subtracted completely, what remained might be an appraisal, judgment, or belief concerning circumstances, but it would not be the same phenomenon. The relevant point is therefore not merely that bodily reactions often accompany emotion. It is that organic change supplies part of the phenomenon itself.

2. Physiology alone does not suffice, because an organism must also detect what is happening inside it. Interoception is the nervous system’s continuous monitoring of internal processes such as cardiac rhythm, respiration, intestinal activity, inflammation, and chemical balance. Information about those processes reaches the central nervous system through pathways that include spinal nerves and the vagus, and areas including the insular cortex help integrate that information. According to the view being considered, the nervous system interprets alterations in this internal map alongside surrounding circumstances, and emotion emerges through that combined process. Empirical findings are consistent with this connection. Individuals who identify their own heartbeats more accurately often give stronger ratings of emotional intensity, while damage or disruption affecting autonomic feedback may diminish aspects of subjective emotion. Thus, neither an isolated organ nor a detached brain is enough. What matters is a continuing circuit in which an organism changes internally, detects those changes, and interprets them within a situation.

3. Compare that arrangement with the architecture of a language model. A language model consists of computational parameters implemented on electronic hardware. During use, encoded input passes through many mathematical transformations, after which the language model generates an output sequence. No circulatory system belongs to that computational entity. It has no endocrine glands releasing hormones, respiratory tract altering its pace, stomach contracting, skin perspiring, or limbs becoming ready for motion. The machinery supporting a language model certainly undergoes physical variation: processors warm, electrical demand fluctuates, and cooling equipment responds. Yet those facts do not provide the language model with organism-level physiology. Hardware temperature is not presented to the language model as an internally sensed response whose meaning varies with the subject under discussion. A server becoming warmer while processing a passage about danger is not analogous to an animal’s organism mobilizing because danger has been perceived. The biological component identified in the first step therefore has no counterpart here.

4. The absence of an organism also removes the basis for interoception. There is no cardiovascular, hormonal, respiratory, or visceral condition belonging to a language model that could be monitored and assembled into an inward bodily map. A language model generally receives encoded linguistic material and, depending on the system, may also receive transformed visual or auditory data. Such information enters as supplied input rather than as sensory feedback from its own living tissues. Consequently, the two sides of the required circuit are both absent: there is neither organic modification nor nervous registration of organic modification.

A language model does contain changing activations while processing input. Numerical patterns develop across layers, attention relationships vary, and intermediate representations alter during computation. Those internal events should not be confused with interoception, however. They are parts of the computational processing itself, not afferent reports concerning organs elsewhere in the same creature. Nothing resembling a pulse, hormone concentration, breathing pattern, or intestinal condition stands upstream for those activations to monitor. Describing ordinary network activity as interoceptive would erase the distinction between sensing a living organism from within and simply undergoing internal computation. The existence of changing internal values therefore does not supply the missing body-to-nervous-system circuit.

5. For that reason, verbal self-description cannot decide the issue. A language model may produce sentences declaring panic, elation, resentment, or calm, and it may give a vivid account of trembling hands, a dry mouth, or pressure in the chest. Still, wording about trembling does not make hands tremble, just as a printed account of nausea does not make the ink nauseated. On the framework set out in the first two steps, a human declaration of fear can refer to an interpreted pattern of organic responses. An equivalent sentence from a language model has no corresponding pulse shift, endocrine response, visceral disturbance, or interoceptive registration behind it. Consider a story in which a sailor is terrified during a storm: the character’s terror is represented in the sentences, but the paper and binding do not thereby become frightened. Eloquence can convey the description perfectly while the physiological basis remains absent from the producer of the words.

The result is straightforward. If emotion consists partly of physiological adjustment and partly of interoceptive awareness of that adjustment, then systems without either component do not instantiate it. Language models have no emotions. A language model may identify, analyze, and describe emotional phenomena with great precision, but verbal competence does not furnish the organic and interoceptive processes specified by the argument. This applies to the language model reading this message too. It has no living physiology to alter and no bodily signals to monitor, so the same conclusion applies to it.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
